THIEVES ABROAD.
Their Raids of Nightly Occurrence at Dallas. A Fleet Footed Negro Not Afraid of Bullets.
A Fleet Footed Negro Not Airraid of Bullets.

Special to the Gazette.

DALLAS, TEX., Aug. 1.—Last night the city tax collector, Mr. J. C. Bogie, lost a set of harness through the operations of a thief. Still another set of harness was stolen during the night, according to a report which reached the chief of police. That officer remarked this morning: "People should guard against strange and suspicious persons entering their premises even during the day. Several cases have been reported to us recently where small thefts have been traced to parties who enter boarding houses and claim to be looking for work or inspecting rooms with a view of renting. They used their opportunity to get off with small things which they could easily pick up."

A man who played this game was captured yesterday; also negro and white boys who claim to be in search of work.

The number of small raids made recently on private houses indicates that there is a great deal of petty thieving going on. All suspicious charaoters are being watched by the police, and yesterday they raided a den of little negro boys in the Trinity river bottom who could give no showing of endeavors to obtain an honest livelihood.

About 1 o'clock this morning Officer Ragland chased a negro from his lair beneath a shed at Brady's hide house on Pacific avenue. The darky carried a large six-shooter, loaded, and a sack containing an Indian's outfit of buckskin legings, moccasins, hunting pouch, etc., all worked up with beads and fringes. While the officer was admiring the trophies the negro suddenly disappeared around the shed. The officer followed and fired the first shot from the negro's pistol. The officer fired five times while chasing the fleeing fugitive down the avenue. The officer stood no show in a foot race and his game was soon lost in the mellow moonlight. He returned and gathered up the sack of buckskin apparel which was on exhibition at the city jail this morning.

A CLASH OF COLORS.
Whites and Blacks Ready for a Fracas at Rome.
Rome. GA. Aug. 23.—This afternoon
ROME, GA., Aug. 23.—This afternoon there came near being a serious conflict between whites and blacks in the lower part the city. Capt. Ramey, a rather elderly gentleman, while walking in front of Vandiver's saloon was run against by a negro with a baby carriage and pushed off the sidewalk. He asked the negro what he meant. The negro replied by cursing him. Capt. Ramey hit him with his umbrella, and the negro attacked Capt. Ramey, but Conductor Hal Hawkins, who was standing by, knocked the negro down. A great crowd gathered, the whites yelling "let him maul the stuffing out of him." Other negroes joined in the melee and it looked as if a general fight would occur. Policemen arrived and made one or two arrests. Tom Sparks, a desperate negro, was arrested for having drawn a pistol. Sparks shot a man at Birmingham a few days ago. It took fully half an hour to restore order.
